title: Treasuring in Heaven vs. Earth
english: They are no longer. But the man is living. Even if he should die, he still lives. Or in this way: a man living who does not become outside of human life is himself vanity; so that it is thus: 'except all things are vanity and every living man' (Eccl 1:2). Or in this way: 'except all things are vanity, but the man is living'. Beyond this: the essence? Even if the man lives differently than a mortal would live, in view of the excellence and the greatness of the divine life and of God himself, the fountain of life, he is nothing.

The small things and the things no smaller than small are said in relation to something. And the small does not have a limited amount; for it is said in reference to the greater. We say, for instance, that the wrestler is greater than the boxer. Indeed, you have in categories a small mountain and a large gulf. 'But indeed, a man wanders in an image' (Eccl 1:14). I said that he speaks about the others besides the man, saying that 'all is vanity'. Only the man is living. And he has more than the others. He has an immortal soul.

However, even if he is living, he does not always have this motion; 'but indeed', for he says, 'a man wanders in an image' (Eccl 1:14). He did not say whether he wanders in praise or in mockery; but however anyone wanders, however he acts, he is in some image. Taking it more generally, it is to be said that it is either of the heavenly or of the earthly. And it is shown from such a word that the man is self-determining; for if he were good by construction, he would always wander in the heavenly, if he were evil by essence, in the earthly.

And it is possible to divide these general images into kinds. And I say that one is in the image of a fox, another in the image of a lion, and a certain mare becoming a horse carrying another image, and another in the image of a dove, except 'in an image every man wanders'. 'But indeed, a man wanders in an image' (Eccl 1:14), except vainly they are troubled. But the worthless are vainly troubled. 'Except vainly they are troubled'. And he therefore speaks of the vain trouble, because this striving concerning human things is such. For instance, he 'stores up' 'and does not know to whom he gathers them' (Eccl 2:18). He stores up and does not know to whom he gathers them. In Ecclesiastes it was clearly said that: 'he does not know whether he will be wise' (Eccl 2:19), the successor of those who are.

His [words] 'or fools'. And often what one has treasured, he leaves behind. Sometimes, as a year passes, he falls away into other things. Therefore, it is not necessary to be anxious about treasuring in this way; for 'lawless treasures will not profit, but righteousness rescues from death' (Prov 11:4). Therefore, the righteousness that rescues from death and from every other evil is to be treasured. This wealth is treasured in heaven.

'Do not treasure for yourselves treasures on earth, but treasure treasures in heaven' (Matt 6:19-21); because where the treasure is, there also the mind is, which is called the 'heart'. It is to be treasured in heaven so that we may have the mind there, and one should refrain from treasuring on earth, so that we may not have the intellect there. It is said concerning some: 'those treasuring injustice and misery in their lands'.

The man, therefore, wandering in an image, treasuring, did not know to whom he was bringing them; for it is unclear to him what he will bequeath. Therefore, the diligent one hears to treasure in the heavens. He has wealth set aside in good works. This is also what Paul writes to Timothy: 'command the rich of this age not to be high-minded concerning wealth, but in God, who provides all things' (1 Tim 6:17).

It must also be said concerning false wealth, such as the heretical opinion of the dogmas of the atheists. And he who treasures these things did not know to whom he was bringing them. But he leaves them to another; for until the present life, he holds the promise of 'the pseudonymous knowledge' (1 Tim 6:20); for when the truth shines forth, it is dissolved and vanishes.

And what about 'only in an image'?—even if every man is living, he is not living without transgression in the praiseworthy living. For if he had remained in the true image, the first, according to which he was created, he would not have been troubled, nor would he have treasured in vain. But indeed, even if he has become living, he wanders in an image; and not altogether in the first, but rather wandering in an image; for never can the rational animal be able to act outside of acting according to reason. And acting, he acts either praiseworthily or falsely, thinking and doing certain things and certain others.

And what about 'but in vain they are troubled'?—it has often already been said to us that these changes occur in such a way. When they do not guard this image according to which they have become, they are a multitude of the vain.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Discipline of Correction and the Escape from Punishment
english: They are being disturbed. When he signifies the life of man, he says, 'every man lives' (Ps 39:1), and 'yet a man wanders in an image'—not in the same one, but because the images are diverse, and especially because many are false and deceptive, many are being disturbed. And now, what is my stability? Is it not the Lord? Regarding others, the things spoken have been said. But as for myself, I say: 'What is my stability? Is it not the Lord?' (Ps 39:17) I do not wait for another. And just as 'wisdom, righteousness, and sanctification become' those who participate, so also stability becomes to the one waiting, the Lord himself. And my subsistence is with you. Concerning the Lord, he says that his stability is. But toward the Lord, who is, he says his subsistence is: 'and my subsistence is with you' (Ps 39:18). It is possible to call subsistence here the strength by which one is able to stand, because, with you cooperating and being my stability, I stand against all things. And the 'subsistence from you' is a praise to me. And it is possible to call subsistence instead of essence. And my subsistence of the rational soul, of the rational animal, is with you; for you have given me a soul; from you I have the soul, not beginning from seeds, not being composed according to an opinion like the Stoic school, but 'my subsistence is from you' (Ps 39:18).

Save me from all my lawlessness (Ps 39:19). Not from some, but 'from all,' so that I may become outside of every false image. A reproach of foolishness you have given me (Ps 39:20). From the beginning we said that the whole psalm bears the face of one repenting and progressing. It is a trivial thing to be reproached by a righteous man, but to be praised by a fool. For the fool indeed reproaches regarding good works and with zeal. For this reason, even in proverbs, as if there were no difference, reproaches are mentioned: 'Do not acquire the reproach of evil men' (Prov 22:8); for he did not say at all, 'Do not acquire reproach,' but 'of evil men.' Do not reproach regarding triviality; for there are those being reproached regarding good things. To the well-known, Jesus says: 'Rejoice and be glad when they reproach you' (Matt 5:11). This kind of reproach is not to be rejected; for it is good and will lead into the kingdom of heaven. But the reproaches of evil men are to be fled from. I was made mute and I did not open my mouth (Ps 39:21). Who is the foolish reproacher, or he is the sinner who stands against him, as...

"He became mute and did not open his mouth"? And here again the same thing is signified: "I became mute and did not open my mouth." He did not answer him regarding what he reproaches. This is often said by another power, as the apostle teaches this, saying: "Reprove not a contentious man for one exhortation" (Prov 9:8). Do not open the mouth to him at all. But so that you may have a defense and a word to say about yourself, "I have done this by myself," exhort him. If he does not submit to the exhortation, or "and a second"—for some manuscripts have "and a second"—overthrow him, "knowing that he sins." One who is "self-condemning" should not be set against.

10–11 For you are the one who made me, turn away your whips from me. Do not lash me; for I am your handiwork. "But he lashes every son whom he receives" (Heb 12:6), having it clear through which he is lashed. Therefore, leave these things to me; grant me a remission, for in this way I shall no longer be lashed. Now I am still liable for the lashings. 278 Therefore, he who has placed the Most High as his refuge (Ps 91:2) has no approaching evils nor a whip approaching his tent. Make me therefore such that I am no longer liable for the lashings; turn away the thing that punishes me. Since therefore I say, "Deliver me from all my iniquities" (Ps 51:2), when you deliver me, I am no longer liable for punishment.

He was lashing him in a certain way even through the thoughtless man, and says that the reproaches of the thoughtless are the lashes. Unless God delivers, one is not able even by opposing that which has not been delivered. 11 From the strength of your hand I have failed (Ps 31:9). The strength of your hand, the educational one, the striking one, the one subjecting to pains, presses upon me. Since therefore it has become strong against me, I have failed. I cast away my former life, I left my former state; for I did not fail so as to no longer exist, or to become weak, but so as to fail the state preparing to punish me. "I have failed." I, saying these things, confessing, saying, "You have given me reproach through thoughtlessness," have failed, having become outside of my former state. It is possible to fail praiseworthily, and it is possible to fail shamefully. "And Esau came from the field, leaving behind" (Gen 25:29), when he desired to eat a meal. The "leaving behind" here is instead of "having grown weak" and "longing for food." It is said often...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The distinction between fleshly, psychic, and spiritual states
english: spiritual

If one attempts things that are different—and one is true and the other is false—one knows from the attempt at opposites which is true and which is false. Indeed, the true itself appears by the showing of the false, because knowledge is of the opposites.

"And you searched out his soul like a spider" (Ps 90:8). You searched out his soul like a spider, his soul according to which he is psychic. Concerning someone bad it is said, "he was carried by the desires of his soul." When someone reshapes [things] from the soul, let it be said, as if they were prophecies or as if they were doctrines of piety, "he is carried by the desires of the soul"; he is not carried by the Holy Spirit.

In another book I have stated the difference: that man is fleshly, he who fights according to the flesh, he who follows the desires of the flesh, he who is driven by the flesh, he who has become fleshly and is driven by sin. But a man is spiritual who has ascended above the psychic state, when he carries everything by the Holy Spirit and by God-bearing, doing and practicing [them]. And psychic is he who is neither fleshly nor spiritual.

And perhaps all the wise of the world are such. They think themselves self-sufficient according to the movements and thoughts of their own souls. And because of this they do not receive the things of the Spirit; for they prefer their own and think their own understanding to be great, they do not receive the foolishness of the Spirit, regarding it as such. And indeed there are certain heresies established in their entirety, both among the Greeks and among the Christians, which say that allegories are foolishnesses, they are mere fabrications. And they say that the theorems concerning the intelligible are false, since they think all things to be bodies and sensible.

These, therefore, are psychic men, not receiving the things of the Spirit, regarding themselves as self-sufficient and capable of contemplating all things by themselves. His soul, then, such a soul—not the essence, but the state according to which it is a soul—you searched out like a spider. And the spider is very weak, as it is said, "they weave a spider's web; their web shall not be a garment" (Job 8:14). The fragility of the construction of the animal...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
